q: Matter is made up of tiny particles, which can be atoms or molecules.
e: The textbook states that all substances are matter and matter is made up of tiny particles, which can be atoms or molecules.

q: Plasma is a hot ionised gas containing charged particles.
e: Plasma is recognized as a fourth state of matter, described as a hot ionised gas containing charged particles.

q: The particles in a solid are packed very tightly together with weak forces between one another.
e: The particles in a solid are packed very tightly together with strong forces between one another.

q: Solids have a definite shape and volume.
e: Because particles in a solid have little freedom of movement and vibrate about a fixed position, solids have a definite shape and volume.

q: Unlike gases, solids cannot be compressed and do not flow.
e: These are common properties of all solids due to the strong forces holding their particles in fixed positions.

q: Solids do not expand when heated.
e: Solids do expand slightly when heated as the particles vibrate more strongly.

q: Liquids are composed of particles which are fixed in definite positions as in solids.
e: Liquids are composed of particles which are not fixed in any definite positions, allowing them to move freely throughout the liquid.

q: Liquids can have a definite volume because the particles in liquid are held together more strongly than those in gases.
e: The stronger attractive forces in liquids compared to gases allow them to maintain a definite volume.

q: Unlike gases, liquids cannot be compressed but they can flow easily.
e: Liquids cannot be compressed due to particle proximity, but they can flow easily because particles are not fixed in position.

q: The particles in a gas are in constant and rapid motion because of strong attractive forces between gaseous particles.
e: The particles in a gas are in constant and rapid motion because of weak attractive forces between gaseous particles.

q: Gases do not have a definite volume and shape of their own.
e: Gas particles move freely and spread out to occupy the whole space of the container, taking its shape and volume.

q: All gases can easily be compressed and spread in all directions.
e: Due to weak attractive forces and large spaces between particles, all gases can easily be compressed and spread in all directions.

q: Brownian motion is the continuous random movement of small particles suspended in a gas or liquid.
e: Brownian motion arises from collisions with the gas or liquid particles, such as the motion of pollen grains on still water.

q: Brownian motion arises from collisions with the solid container walls only.
e: Brownian motion arises from collisions with the gas or liquid particles, not just the container walls.

q: Diffusion is mainly seen in solids and liquids.
e: Diffusion is mainly seen in liquids and gases, where particles have more freedom of movement.

q: In diffusion, the particles of one substance mix with and move through the particles of another substance.
e: This is the exact definition of the diffusion process as described in the textbook.

q: The bigger the mass of particles, the faster the particles diffuse.
e: The bigger the mass, the slower the particles diffuse; the smaller the mass, the faster they diffuse.

q: The higher the temperature, it enables the particles to diffuse faster.
e: Higher temperatures provide particles with more kinetic energy, enabling them to diffuse faster.

q: The air, the sea water, and alloys are pure substances.
e: The air, sea water, and alloys are not pure substances; they are mixtures.

q: Adding sugar to tea or coffee is a solid-liquid mixture.
e: This process involves a solid (sugar) mixing with a liquid (tea or coffee), forming a solid-liquid mixture.

q: A physical change is a change in which no new substances are formed.
e: In a physical change, there may be a temporary change in colour, temperature, or state, but no new substances are formed.

q: Melting, boiling, freezing, evaporation, vaporisation, condensation and sublimation are considered as chemical changes.
e: These processes are considered physical changes because no new chemical substances are formed.

q: The temperature at which a solid melts is called the melting point.
e: The melting point is the specific temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid state at one atmospheric pressure.

q: When a solid substance is heated, the particles of the solid vibrate more weakly.
e: When a solid substance is heated, the particles of the solid vibrate more strongly until they overcome the forces holding them.

q: Vaporisation is the process that occurs when a chemical or element is converted from a liquid to a vapour.
e: Vaporisation involves liquid particles gaining enough energy to break forces holding them together and escape to the space above.

q: Evaporation is the process of a substance in a gaseous state changing to a liquid state due to a decrease in temperature.
e: Evaporation is the process of a substance in a liquid state changing to a gaseous state due to an increase in temperature and/or pressure.

q: Boiling is the rapid vaporisation of a liquid, which occurs when a liquid is heated to its boiling point.
e: Boiling is defined as rapid vaporisation occurring specifically at the boiling point of the liquid.

q: Sublimation is the change of liquid state directly into gaseous state.
e: Sublimation is the change of solid state directly into gaseous state without melting.

q: Deposition is the direct solidification of a vapour by cooling.
e: Deposition is the reverse of sublimation, where water vapour turns directly to frost, for example.

q: A chemical change is a change in which one or more new substances are formed.
e: In a chemical change, substances change in colour, temperature, and state, and also change into a new substance or substances.

q: Cooking of rice from rice grains and burning of a match are examples of physical changes.
e: Cooking of rice and burning of a match are examples of chemical changes because new substances are formed.

q: Heating of limestone or marble is an example of dissociation or decomposition.
e: Heating limestone ($CaCO_3$) causes it to break down, which is a chemical change classified as dissociation or decomposition.

q: Use of magnesia to treat gastric patient is an example of precipitation.
e: Use of magnesia to treat a gastric patient is an example of neutralisation, not precipitation.

q: Passing carbon dioxide into lime water is an example of precipitation.
e: Passing carbon dioxide into lime water causes it to become cloudy, which is a chemical change known as precipitation.

q: The temperature at which the vapour pressure of the liquid is equal to the atmospheric pressure of the surrounding is called the boiling point.
e: This is the exact definition of the boiling point provided in the key terms.

q: Freezing is the process in which a liquid becomes sufficiently cold to change into a solid.
e: Freezing point is the temperature at which this change from liquid to solid occurs.

q: Condensation is the change from a liquid state to its gaseous state.
e: Condensation is the change from a gaseous state to its liquid state.

q: Sublimation is the change of solid state directly into gaseous state without melting.
e: An example given is iodine solid changing to iodine vapour when gently heated.

q: All samples of matter can be divided into two categories: pure substances and mixtures.
e: Pure substances have a definite and constant composition, while mixtures do not.

q: A pure substance is a form of matter that always has a variable composition.
e: A pure substance is a form of matter that always has a definite and constant composition.

q: John Dalton proposed the theory of matter at the beginning of the 19th century.
e: Dalton proposed that all matter was composed of atoms, which were invisible and indivisible.

q: According to John Dalton, atoms were visible and divisible.
e: John Dalton proposed that atoms were invisible and indivisible.

q: Modern experimental evidence has shown that atoms are indivisible.
e: Modern experimental evidence has shown that atoms are divisible to create either lighter or heavier atoms.

q: The atom is still considered as the basic unit of any element.
e: An atom may combine chemically to form molecules, but the atom remains the basic unit of an element.

q: A molecule is the smallest unit of any substances that possesses the properties of that substance.
e: Molecules can exist in elements as well as compounds.

q: Elements are substances consisting of more than one type of atom.
e: Elements are substances consisting of one type of atom, e.g., carbon element is made up of carbon atoms.

q: There are 92 known elements which occur naturally.
e: These elements occur naturally, either in the free or combined state.
